(CNN) -- U.N. Secretary-General Ban Ki-moon has urged the leaders of Madagascar to resolve their differences after an anti-government rally a day earlier turned violent and left more than two dozen people dead. Protesters rally Saturday before violence broke out near the Presidential Palace. In a statement issued by his spokesperson, Ban deplored the violence and called Sunday on authorities "to urgently initiate a fair process by which those responsible will be brought to justice." Ban also blamed the "tragedy" on a "lack of restraint on all sides." "The Secretary-General calls upon all concerned parties to resolve their differences through peaceful and democratic means and through the exercise of responsible leadership," according to the statement. A police official said the death toll from Saturday's violence outside the Presidential Palace in the capital city of Antananarivo had risen to 26. More than 80 were injured during the demonstration, officials said. The capital city was quiet as mourners attended a public ceremony for the dead. The violence stemmed from an ongoing dispute over who is in charge of the government. Andry Rajoelina, the mayor of Antananarivo, took to the streets one week ago, declaring himself the Indian Ocean island nation's leader after a week of violence and looting that killed at least 80 people and wounded more than 300. Rajoelina had called the rally to unveil his new government at the May 13th Plaza, according to Brittany Martin, an American citizen who is a Harvard Fellow and lives in Antananarivo. Martin said the rally was peaceful in the morning hours of Saturday, until gunshots rang out in the afternoon after the protesters marched from the plaza to the palace. She said it was unclear where the shots were coming from. Some media reports blamed foreign mercenaries for the shootings; others said army guards were responsible or that the army was firing at the mercenaries to protect the crowd. Violence in Madagascar began January 26, when protesters stormed state-run television and radio stations in Antananarivo. Hours earlier, the government had shut down a radio station owned by Rajoelina and, weeks ago, had similarly shut down Rajoelina's television station after it aired an interview with ex-President Didier Ratsiraka.  See pictures from last week's upheaval » . Ravalomanana took power in 2001 after ousting Ratsiraka in a tense, hotly contested election. Ratsiraka fled to France afterward. Loyalists blame Ratsiraka's family members for inciting the recent trouble. Anger has risen in Madagascar, where the World Bank says the average person earns about $320 a year, over reports that Ravalomanana recently bought a $60 million airplane. Rajoelina has urged supporters to demand the resignation of Ravalomanana and said he planned to take charge until a transition government could be established in the nation off Africa's southeastern coast. He said he had received reports that palace guards used tear gas and shot into the air to try and disperse the crowd. (CNN) — U.N. Secretary-General Ban Ki-moon appealed to Madagascar’s political leaders to settle their dispute peacefully after an opposition demonstration near the Presidential Palace turned deadly the previous day.

Through a statement released by his spokesperson on Sunday, Ban condemned the bloodshed and urged officials “to urgently initiate a fair process by which those responsible will be brought to justice.” He attributed the “tragedy” to a “lack of restraint on all sides.”

“The Secretary-General calls upon all concerned parties to resolve their differences through peaceful and democratic means and through the exercise of responsible leadership,” the statement said.

A police official reported that 26 people had died in Saturday’s violence outside the Presidential Palace in Antananarivo, Madagascar’s capital. Officials said more than 80 others were wounded. The city was calm Sunday as people gathered for a public memorial honoring those killed.

The unrest arose from a continuing struggle over control of the government. One week earlier, Antananarivo Mayor Andry Rajoelina had taken to the streets and proclaimed himself leader of the Indian Ocean island nation. His declaration followed a week of looting and violence in which at least 80 people were killed and more than 300 injured.

President Marc Ravalomanana subsequently dismissed Rajoelina as mayor and appointed a replacement.

According to Brittany Martin, a U.S. citizen, Harvard Fellow and Antananarivo resident, Rajoelina organized Saturday’s gathering at May 13th Plaza to announce his new government. Martin said the event remained peaceful during the morning. Violence erupted later in the day, after demonstrators marched from the plaza toward the palace and gunfire was heard. She said the source of the shots was uncertain.

News accounts offered conflicting explanations. Some blamed foreign mercenaries, while others alleged that army guards opened fire. Still other reports suggested troops were shooting at mercenaries in an attempt to protect the demonstrators.

The latest turmoil in Madagascar began January 26, when protesters seized government-operated television and radio facilities in Antananarivo. Earlier that day, authorities had closed a radio station belonging to Rajoelina. Several weeks before that, the government had also taken his television station off the air after it broadcast an interview with former President Didier Ratsiraka.

Ravalomanana came to power in 2001 after defeating and removing Ratsiraka following a bitterly disputed election. Ratsiraka later fled to France. Supporters of Ravalomanana have accused members of Ratsiraka’s family of provoking the recent unrest.

Public resentment has also intensified over reports that Ravalomanana recently purchased a $60 million aircraft. According to the World Bank, the average annual income in Madagascar is approximately $320.

Rajoelina has called on his followers to press for Ravalomanana’s resignation. He has also said he intends to lead the country, located off Africa’s southeastern coast, until a transitional government can be formed.

Rodney Ford, a spokesperson for the U.S. Embassy, said, “What we’ve been pushing for is dialogue the whole time.” He added that he had received accounts indicating palace guards used tear gas and fired shots into the air in an effort to break up the crowd.

counterfactuals.output:
# Madagascar political crisis deepens after deadly palace shooting

**ANTANANARIVO, Madagascar —** Madagascar’s political standoff intensified after presidential guards opened fire on opposition supporters marching toward a presidential palace in the capital, killing at least 28 people and wounding scores more, according to local officials and hospital workers.

The February 7, 2009, bloodshed at the Ambohitsorohitra palace became a turning point in the escalating dispute between President Marc Ravalomanana and opposition leader Andry Rajoelina, the former mayor of Antananarivo.

Thousands of demonstrators had gathered in the capital before moving toward the palace, where opposition figures said they intended to install a new prime minister. Security forces warned the crowd not to enter a restricted area before gunfire erupted. Witnesses described scenes of panic as protesters fled and the wounded were carried away.

The precise death toll was disputed, but the killings fueled public anger and sharpened calls for Ravalomanana to step down.

Rajoelina accused the president of authoritarian rule, corruption and mismanagement. He declared that Ravalomanana was no longer fit to govern and positioned himself as the head of a rival administration. The government, in turn, accused Rajoelina of attempting to seize power outside constitutional channels.

The confrontation had been building for weeks. Ravalomanana’s government shut down a television station owned by Rajoelina after it broadcast an interview with exiled former President Didier Ratsiraka. Rajoelina then led mass protests and was removed as mayor by the authorities.

As demonstrations, strikes and looting spread, the political struggle drew increasing concern from the international community.

United Nations Secretary-General Ban Ki-moon called on both sides to exercise restraint, avoid further violence and resolve the crisis through peaceful dialogue. The United Nations and African mediators pressed the rival camps to negotiate, warning that continued confrontation could deepen instability in the Indian Ocean nation.

The crisis ultimately reached a climax in March 2009, when Ravalomanana stepped down under mounting pressure and transferred authority to the military. The military then handed power to Rajoelina. The African Union and other international bodies condemned the transfer as unconstitutional and suspended Madagascar from regional organizations.

The palace deaths remained one of the darkest episodes of the crisis, symbolizing the human cost of a power struggle that fractured Madagascar’s political institutions and left the country internationally isolated.

counterfactuals.prompt: Explain the violence in Madagascar involving President Marc Ravalomanana and opposition leader Andry Rajoelina, with details about the rally, casualty figures, eyewitness accounts, and international reaction.
counterfactuals.output:
The violence occurred on **7 February 2009** in Madagascar’s capital, **Antananarivo**, during an escalating confrontation between President **Marc Ravalomanana** and opposition leader **Andry Rajoelina**, the recently removed mayor of the capital.

### The rally and shooting

Rajoelina had accused Ravalomanana of corruption, authoritarianism, and using state institutions to suppress opponents. After declaring that the president was no longer legitimate, he announced a rival transitional administration and called supporters to a rally in Antananarivo’s **13 May Square**.

Following the rally, thousands of demonstrators marched toward the **Ambohitsorohitra presidential palace**, an official presidential compound in the city center. Opposition representatives intended to install Rajoelina’s designated prime minister there. When the crowd approached or crossed the palace security perimeter, presidential guards opened fire.

Witnesses described sustained bursts of automatic gunfire and demonstrators collapsing or fleeing in panic. Some said there had been little or no effective warning before troops fired directly into the crowd. Journalists and medical workers reported bodies lying in the street and wounded people being carried away in carts, private cars, and ambulances. Other accounts said warning shots had first been fired and that parts of the crowd continued advancing or tried to force their way into the compound.

The government maintained that the palace was a restricted security zone and that guards acted after demonstrators ignored warnings. Rajoelina’s movement characterized the marchers as largely unarmed and called the shooting a deliberate massacre.

### Casualties

Figures varied as hospitals and relief agencies counted casualties:

- Contemporary reports generally put the death toll at **at least 28**.
- About **200 people were wounded**; a commonly cited hospital figure was **212 injured**.
- Some initial Red Cross and hospital reports listed lower totals—around **23 to 25 dead**—before the count rose.

The February 7 deaths were the worst single episode in a broader political crisis that had already produced rioting, looting, and fatalities in January.

### International reaction

The shooting prompted widespread condemnation and calls for restraint:

- **UN Secretary-General Ban Ki-moon** deplored the loss of life and urged both sides to end the violence and settle the crisis through dialogue.
- The **African Union** condemned the bloodshed, pressed the parties to negotiate, and later rejected any unconstitutional transfer of power.
- The **Southern African Development Community**, the **European Union**, the **United States**, and France also appealed for calm and a political settlement.
- International mediators, including representatives of the UN and African regional organizations, attempted to bring Ravalomanana and Rajoelina into negotiations.

The killings badly weakened Ravalomanana’s position. The confrontation continued until **March 2009**, when the military shifted behind Rajoelina, Ravalomanana resigned under pressure, and Rajoelina assumed control of a transitional authority. The African Union and much of the international community treated that transfer as an unconstitutional change of government.
